questions.stem: Which plant group is called the ‘AMPHIBIANS of the plant kingdom’ because they need WATER for their REPRODUCTIVE stage?

options.option_text: BRYOPHYTA — mosses, liverworts, hornworts; they have no vascular tissue; gametes (sperm) swim through water to the egg; thrive in moist shaded places

questions.explanation: BRYOPHYTA — small, non-vascular land plants; called ‘AMPHIBIANS OF THE PLANT KINGDOM’ because: (a) they live on land but (b) REQUIRE WATER for SEXUAL REPRODUCTION (sperms are flagellated and SWIM through a thin film of water to reach the egg). Three classes: (1) HEPATICOPSIDA / Liverworts (e.g., MARCHANTIA); (2) ANTHOCEROPSIDA / Hornworts; (3) BRYOPSIDA / MOSSES (e.g., FUNARIA, SPHAGNUM/peat moss). CHARACTERISTICS: (1) No TRUE ROOTS, STEMS, LEAVES — have rhizoids, axes, leaf-like structures (thalloid/leafy body). (2) No VASCULAR TISSUE — no xylem/phloem → limited in size (mostly <10 cm). (3) GAMETOPHYTE (n) is the DOMINANT generation; sporophyte (2n) grows on gametophyte, is short-lived. (4) ALTERNATION of generations (as in all plants). PLANT KINGDOM OVERVIEW (WHITTAKER's 5 kingdoms + Whittaker's division of plants): (I) THALLOPHYTA (algae) — simplest, water-living, no true tissues. Includes CHLOROPHYCEAE (green algae — Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra, Ulva), RHODOPHYCEAE (red — Gracilaria, Porphyra — source of AGAR, carrageenan), PHAEOPHYCEAE (brown — Kelp, Fucus, Sargassum — largest algae). (II) BRYOPHYTA (mosses/liverworts) — amphibians. (III) PTERIDOPHYTA (ferns, horsetails, club mosses) — FIRST vascular plants (xylem + phloem); no seeds; reproduce by SPORES; e.g., DRYOPTERIS (fern), EQUISETUM (horsetail), SELAGINELLA, PSILOTUM. (IV) GYMNOSPERMS (‘naked seed’) — SEED plants where seed is NOT enclosed in a fruit; CONIFEROUS plants (pines, spruce, fir, cedar, deodar, redwood, cycas, ginkgo, gnetum); most conifers are EVERGREEN with NEEDLE-shaped leaves; dominant in boreal (taiga) forests. (V) ANGIOSPERMS (‘enclosed seed’) — FLOWERING plants, seed enclosed in fruit; ~3,00,000 species — largest plant group. Subdivided into DICOTS (2 seed-leaves/cotyledons; e.g. bean, rose, mango, neem; reticulate leaves, tap root, 4-5 petals) and MONOCOTS (1 cotyledon; e.g. rice, wheat, maize, onion, banana, lily, palm; parallel venation, fibrous roots, 3 petals).

questions.stem: Which plant group bears ‘NAKED SEEDS’, i.e., seeds NOT enclosed within a fruit?

options.option_text: GYMNOSPERMS — Greek ‘gymnos’ (naked) + ‘sperma’ (seed); includes pines, firs, cedars, cycas, ginkgo; mostly evergreen; seeds on cone scales

questions.explanation: GYMNOSPERMS (Greek gymnos = ‘naked’ + sperma = ‘seed’) — seed plants whose seeds DEVELOP exposed on the SURFACE of modified structures (cone scales or similar), NOT enclosed in an ovary/fruit. First seed plants in evolution (~360 million years ago, Carboniferous). 4 main DIVISIONS: (1) CONIFEROPHYTA (Conifers) — largest; includes pines, firs, spruces, cedars, redwoods, larches, junipers, cypresses; dominate BOREAL / TAIGA FORESTS of Northern Hemisphere; most are EVERGREEN with needle-shaped leaves and resinous wood; famous ones: PINUS (pine), CEDRUS DEODARA (Himalayan cedar — Indian ‘deodar’, national tree of Pakistan), SEQUOIADENDRON GIGANTEUM (Giant Sequoia, largest organisms by volume), PINUS LONGAEVA (bristlecone pine, Earth's oldest trees, some >4,800 years), JUNIPERUS. (2) CYCADOPHYTA (Cycads) — primitive palm-like; CYCAS; often called ‘LIVING FOSSILS’. (3) GINKGOPHYTA — only 1 living species: GINKGO BILOBA (maidenhair tree, native China; surviving for 200+ million years — another living fossil; widely planted). (4) GNETOPHYTA — small group; GNETUM, EPHEDRA (source of ephedrine), WELWITSCHIA (bizarre Namibian desert plant). ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE: (a) TIMBER — 80% of world's softwood comes from conifers (pine, fir, spruce); (b) PAPER & PULP — mostly spruce and pine; (c) RESIN — turpentine, rosin; (d) FOOD — pine nuts, ginkgo nuts; (e) MEDICINE — Taxol anti-cancer from PACIFIC YEW (Taxus); Ephedrine from Ephedra; (f) ORNAMENTAL — Christmas trees (fir/spruce), landscaping. ANGIOSPERMS (flowering plants) evolved ~140 million years ago and have now overtaken gymnosperms in species (~3,00,000 vs ~1,000) and are DOMINANT in most biomes except boreal forests. Key DIFFERENCES Angio vs Gymno: (1) seeds enclosed in fruit vs naked on cones; (2) double fertilisation (angio only — one sperm fuses with egg → zygote; another with polar nuclei → endosperm triploid); (3) angios have flowers; (4) angios have vessels (xylem); gymnos have tracheids only (usually); (5) angios have specialised phloem sieve elements + companion cells; (6) life cycle shorter typically in angio.

questions.stem: The site of photosynthesis within a plant cell is the:

options.option_text: CHLOROPLAST — an organelle containing CHLOROPHYLL (green pigment) + enzymes (RuBisCO); contains its own DNA + ribosomes (endosymbiont origin)

questions.explanation: CHLOROPLAST — the organelle responsible for PHOTOSYNTHESIS in plant and algal cells; type of PLASTID (other plastids: chromoplast for pigments, leucoplast for storage — amyloplast stores starch, elaioplast oils, proteoplast proteins). STRUCTURE of chloroplast (lens-shaped, 3-10 μm): (1) OUTER + INNER MEMBRANES (double membrane like mitochondria; hence endosymbiont origin — ancestral cyanobacterium engulfed by proto-eukaryote 1.5 bya). (2) STROMA — fluid-filled matrix; site of CALVIN CYCLE (dark/light-independent reactions). (3) THYLAKOIDS — stack of flat membrane sacs (1 stack = GRANUM); site of LIGHT REACTIONS; contains PHOTOSYSTEMS (PS I, PS II) — pigment-protein complexes with CHLOROPHYLL-a, chlorophyll-b, carotenoids. (4) GRANA — stacks of thylakoids; connected by STROMA LAMELLAE. (5) CHLOROPHYLL pigments absorb MAINLY red (~660 nm) + blue (~430 nm) light; REFLECT GREEN → plants appear green. (6) ENDOSYMBIONT origin: chloroplasts have their own CIRCULAR DNA (cpDNA), 70S ribosomes (like bacteria), divide by binary fission — strong evidence that they descended from an ancient cyanobacterium engulfed by an early eukaryote (Lynn Margulis, endosymbiotic theory). Similarly mitochondria descended from an ancient alpha-proteobacterium. Plant leaves contain ~20-100 chloroplasts per mesophyll cell; palisade cells have the most. PIGMENTS: (a) CHLOROPHYLL A (blue-green; main) — C₅₅H₇₂O₅N₄Mg; Mg at centre of porphyrin ring; (b) Chl B (yellow-green; accessory); (c) CAROTENOIDS — β-carotene (orange, precursor of Vit A), xanthophylls (yellow, visible in autumn leaves once chl-a breaks down); (d) PHYCOBILINS in red algae (phycoerythrin red, phycocyanin blue). Different pigments allow plants to capture a wider spectrum of light. ABSORPTION spectrum of chlorophyll matches ACTION spectrum of photosynthesis (peaks in red+blue, trough in green — hence green is the 'reflected, least-used' colour).

questions.stem: The plant hormone that causes RIPENING OF FRUITS (banana, mango, tomato) is:

options.option_text: ETHYLENE — a GASEOUS hormone; emitted by ripening fruits; causes chlorophyll breakdown, softening, starch→sugar, aroma production; commercially used in fruit rooms (ethephon → ethylene)

questions.explanation: ETHYLENE (C₂H₄, ethene) — unique GASEOUS plant hormone, released by ripening fruits. Causes: (1) CHLOROPHYLL breakdown (green → yellow/red/orange); (2) CELL WALL SOFTENING; (3) STARCH → SUGAR conversion; (4) aroma compound production; (5) LEAF abscission (fall of leaves); (6) flower senescence; (7) sex determination in some plants (cucurbits → female flowers). COMMERCIAL USE: (a) FRUITS are often transported GREEN + UNRIPE (harder, longer shelf life), and RIPENED with ETHEPHON (an ethylene-releasing chemical) or direct ethylene gas in special rooms — bananas from Colombia/Ecuador, mangoes for export, tomatoes, avocados. (b) ‘One BAD APPLE spoils the bunch’ — a ripe/rotten apple releases ethylene, causing neighbours to ripen/rot faster; hence store separately. (c) Ethylene INHIBITS growth of non-fruit parts — e.g., keeps flower stems short. FIVE MAJOR CLASSES OF PLANT HORMONES (phytohormones): (1) AUXIN (e.g., INDOLE-3-ACETIC ACID, IAA) — discovered by DARWIN (1880s, CHARLES + FRANCIS) studying phototropism of canary grass; produced in apical meristem; causes CELL ELONGATION, APICAL DOMINANCE (suppresses lateral buds), PHOTOTROPISM (shoots bend toward light), GRAVITROPISM (roots grow down), root initiation from cuttings. Synthetic: IBA, NAA for rooting; 2,4-D as selective broadleaf herbicide; IAA increases parthenocarpy (seedless fruit). (2) GIBBERELLIN (GA) — named after fungus GIBBERELLA FUJIKUROI (causes bakanae ‘foolish seedling’ disease in rice, excessive elongation); causes stem elongation (‘bolting’), seed germination, breaks dormancy, parthenocarpy. Used on grapes to elongate stalks. (3) CYTOKININ (e.g., KINETIN, ZEATIN) — promotes CELL DIVISION (cytokinesis); delays leaf senescence (‘richmond-lang effect’); enhances lateral bud growth (opposes auxin). Used in tissue culture. (4) ABSCISIC ACID (ABA) — STRESS hormone; closes STOMATA under drought; induces dormancy (seeds, buds); inhibits growth; promotes abscission (leaf fall). (5) ETHYLENE — as above. Other growth regulators: BRASSINOSTEROIDS, SYSTEMIN, JASMONATES, SALICYLIC ACID (defence), NITRIC OXIDE, FLORIGEN (flowering).

questions.stem: In plants, XYLEM tissue is responsible for:

options.option_text: TRANSPORT of WATER + dissolved MINERALS from ROOTS to LEAVES — flow is UNIDIRECTIONAL (upward); includes tracheids, vessel elements (dead at maturity)

questions.explanation: XYLEM vs PHLOEM — the two vascular tissues of vascular plants (pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms). XYLEM: (1) Transports WATER and MINERALS (absorbed by roots) upward to leaves and other aerial parts; (2) Unidirectional (bottom → top, driven by TRANSPIRATIONAL PULL at leaves + root pressure + adhesion-cohesion of water); (3) Composed of 4 cell types: (a) TRACHEIDS (elongated, tapered, dead at maturity, present in all vascular plants including gymnosperms + ferns); (b) VESSEL ELEMENTS / VESSELS (shorter, wider, open-ended to form continuous tubes — mainly in ANGIOSPERMS; gymnosperms lack vessels usually); (c) XYLEM PARENCHYMA (living, storage); (d) XYLEM FIBERS (sclerenchyma, strength); (4) Cell walls lignified for structural support; (5) Annual rings in trees (= secondary xylem rings in wood — basis of DENDROCHRONOLOGY). PHLOEM: (1) Transports MANUFACTURED FOOD (mainly SUCROSE, also amino acids, hormones) from leaves (source) to other parts (sinks — growing tips, fruits, storage organs); (2) BIDIRECTIONAL (can flow up or down seasonally); (3) Composed of: (a) SIEVE TUBE ELEMENTS (in angios) or SIEVE CELLS (in gymnos) — elongated, perforated sieve plates at ends, NO nucleus at maturity; (b) COMPANION CELLS (only in angios, closely linked to sieve tubes via plasmodesmata, maintain sieve tube function); (c) PHLOEM PARENCHYMA; (d) PHLOEM FIBERS; (4) ‘PRESSURE FLOW HYPOTHESIS’ (Münch 1930) — loading of sugars at source creates osmotic pressure, driving bulk flow to sink. TREE RINGS: wood of a tree = accumulated SECONDARY XYLEM. Each year, the cambium produces a layer of xylem; SPRINGWOOD (earlywood, light, wide vessels, fast growth) + SUMMERWOOD / AUTUMNWOOD (latewood, dense, narrow, dark) = 1 ring. By counting, age is determined; width indicates climate (wide = favourable, narrow = drought). BARK is outer protective tissue (cork + secondary phloem). HEARTWOOD (inner, darker, dead, non-conducting, structural) vs SAPWOOD (outer, lighter, living, water-conducting).

questions.stem: Which of the following plants exhibits PARTHENOCARPY (formation of fruit WITHOUT fertilisation)?

options.option_text: BANANA, seedless grapes, seedless watermelon, pineapple — fruit develops without fertilisation; hence seedless

questions.explanation: PARTHENOCARPY (Greek: parthenos = virgin, karpos = fruit) — development of FRUIT WITHOUT FERTILISATION, resulting in SEEDLESS fruits. Types: (1) NATURAL (e.g., BANANA, pineapple — cultivated varieties; pineapple is actually a multiple-fruit formed from whole inflorescence); (2) CHEMICALLY INDUCED (applying auxins like NAA, IAA, IBA, or gibberellins to flowers, which trigger fruit development; used commercially for TOMATO, GRAPES, WATERMELON to create seedless versions); (3) GENETIC parthenocarpy (some mutant lines). BENEFITS: seedless fruits fetch higher market price; easier to consume, process (juice, pulp). CAVEATS: such plants may need vegetative propagation (cuttings, grafts, tissue culture) since they cannot produce viable seeds; a disease could wipe out the whole clone (e.g., Panama disease threatening CAVENDISH banana — 99% of export bananas). FORMS of FRUITS (exam favourite): (1) SIMPLE fruit — from one flower, one ovary; (a) FLESHY — drupe (mango, coconut — single seed with hard endocarp), berry (tomato, grape, banana — multiple seeds no hard endocarp), pome (apple, pear — fleshy receptacle, core is actual ovary), hesperidium (orange, lemon — segmented, juicy vesicles), pepo (cucumber, watermelon, pumpkin), (b) DRY — dehiscent (legume/pea, capsule/cotton, silique/mustard), indehiscent (nut/walnut, caryopsis/wheat-rice-maize — grain with fused seed+pericarp, achene/sunflower). (2) AGGREGATE fruit — many ovaries from same flower (strawberry — the red fleshy part is the accessory receptacle, seeds are tiny achenes on surface; raspberry; custard apple). (3) MULTIPLE fruit — fused from many flowers of an inflorescence (pineapple, jackfruit, mulberry). FALSE FRUITS / ACCESSORY FRUITS — fleshy part is not from ovary but from receptacle or other floral parts: APPLE (thalamus/receptacle), STRAWBERRY (receptacle), CASHEW (pedicel); true fruit in cashew is the nut. SEEDLESS WATERMELONS: triploid hybrids (2n female × 4n male → 3n offspring; sterile due to uneven chromosomes but still develop pseudo-fruits).

questions.stem: In ANGIOSPERMS, the unique process of DOUBLE FERTILISATION was first observed by:

options.option_text: SERGEI NAWASCHIN (Russian botanist, 1898) in Lilium and Fritillaria — one sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm

questions.explanation: DOUBLE FERTILISATION — a UNIQUE FEATURE OF ANGIOSPERMS (flowering plants). First observed by SERGEI GAVRILOVICH NAWASCHIN (Ukrainian/Russian botanist) in 1898, in species of LILIUM and FRITILLARIA (lily family). PROCESS: (1) A mature pollen grain contains a TUBE cell + GENERATIVE cell. (2) On the stigma, pollen germinates — pollen tube grows down the style into the ovary. (3) The generative cell divides to form TWO SPERM CELLS that travel via the pollen tube. (4) Pollen tube enters ovule via the MICROPYLE; reaches the embryo sac (female gametophyte, contains EGG CELL + 2 SYNERGIDS + 3 ANTIPODALS + 2 POLAR NUCLEI = 7 cells, 8 nuclei — 8-nucleate Polygonum type, commonest). (5) FIRST FERTILISATION: one sperm (n) fuses with EGG (n) → DIPLOID ZYGOTE (2n) → EMBRYO. This is ‘syngamy’. (6) SECOND FERTILISATION: the OTHER sperm (n) fuses with 2 POLAR NUCLEI (n + n, already fused in some species as central cell) → TRIPLOID PRIMARY ENDOSPERM NUCLEUS (3n) → ENDOSPERM (nutritive tissue for developing embryo). This is ‘triple fusion’. Hence: ‘DOUBLE fertilisation’ (one syngamy + one triple fusion). OUTCOMES: (a) DIPLOID embryo develops into plant; (b) TRIPLOID endosperm stores food reserves (starch in wheat/rice/maize grain = endosperm; coconut water + flesh = liquid + solid endosperm of the coconut fruit); (c) integuments of ovule → seed coat (testa + tegmen); (d) ovary wall → fruit wall (pericarp). IMPORTANCE: (1) ensures endosperm forms only WHEN fertilisation occurs — no wasted resource if no embryo; (2) gives angiosperms an evolutionary advantage over gymnosperms (which form endosperm before fertilisation, wasting resources on unfertilised ovules). Gymnosperms: ONLY SINGLE fertilisation; endosperm is haploid gametophytic tissue stored BEFORE fertilisation; no double fertilisation. SYNGAMY — general term for fusion of two gametes to form zygote (any sexually reproducing organism). TRIPLOID ENDOSPERM: unique to angios; provides energy for embryo germination. In wheat/rice, humans eat the endosperm (+ embryo/germ + bran).

questions.stem: Which plant is known for its INSECT-TRAPPING ability, a classic example of carnivorous behaviour in plants?

options.option_text: NEPENTHES / PITCHER PLANT, Drosera (Sundew), Dionaea muscipula (Venus flytrap), Utricularia (Bladderwort) — these trap + digest insects to obtain NITROGEN (as they grow in nitrogen-poor soils)

questions.explanation: CARNIVOROUS (insectivorous) PLANTS — species adapted to trap and digest INSECTS and other small animals to obtain NITROGEN + phosphorus + minerals that are scarce in their usual habitat (boggy, acidic, nutrient-poor soils). They STILL do photosynthesis for energy; carnivory is just supplementary nutrition. TYPES of TRAPS: (1) PITFALL — NEPENTHES (tropical pitcher plants, SE Asia, Madagascar, India's Khasi hills — NEPENTHES KHASIANA is India's only Nepenthes, endemic to Meghalaya; endangered); Sarracenia (American pitcher plant); Cephalotus; Darlingtonia (cobra lily). Pitcher is a MODIFIED LEAF (hollow, fluid-filled); insects attracted by nectar/colour fall in, can't escape slippery waxy walls, drown, are digested by enzymes (nepenthesin). (2) SNAP / ACTIVE — DIONAEA MUSCIPULA (VENUS FLYTRAP, North Carolina) — leaves modified into bilobed jaws with trigger hairs; snaps shut in ~100 ms when insect touches 2 hairs within 20 sec. (3) FLYPAPER / ADHESIVE — DROSERA (SUNDEW) — leaves have tentacles bearing sticky mucilage drops; insects stick, tentacles curl inward, digestion. Also PINGUICULA (butterwort). (4) SUCTION / BLADDER — UTRICULARIA (BLADDERWORT, aquatic) — tiny bladders with trigger hairs; low pressure inside; trigger causes sudden suction. FASTEST plant movement (<1 ms). (5) LOBSTER-POT — GENLISEA; inward-pointing hairs force prey inward. Charles Darwin wrote ‘Insectivorous Plants’ (1875) on experiments with Drosera. INDIAN CONTEXT: (a) NEPENTHES KHASIANA — ‘Tiew-rakot’ of Khasi, ‘Memang-Koksi’ of Jaintia — endangered, CITES Appendix I; found only in Garo + Khasi + Jaintia hills of Meghalaya. (b) DROSERA species in Western Ghats, Meghalaya, NE. (c) UTRICULARIA globally distributed in freshwater bodies. (d) ALDROVANDA VESICULOSA (waterwheel plant) in Dal Lake, Kashmir. OTHER SPECIAL PLANTS: (e) MIMOSA PUDICA (‘touch-me-not’) — rapid leaf closure upon touch (SEISMONASTIC movement — pulvinus cells lose turgor); (f) BIOPHYTUM SENSITIVUM — similar but slower; (g) SUNFLOWER — HELIOTROPIC (tracks sun); (h) RAFFLESIA — largest single flower in world (~1 m), parasitic on Tetrastigma vines, SE Asia, no leaves/stem/root, infamous ‘corpse flower’ stench; (i) AMORPHOPHALLUS TITANUM (titan arum) — largest unbranched inflorescence, same stench; (j) CUSCUTA (dodder) — parasitic angiosperm, no chlorophyll; wraps around host plants, sucks nutrients via haustoria.

questions.stem: The cellulose of the plant CELL WALL is chemically:

options.option_text: A POLYSACCHARIDE — long UNBRANCHED chain of β-1,4-glucose units; provides RIGIDITY; humans CAN'T digest it (no cellulase enzyme) — it is dietary FIBRE

questions.explanation: CELLULOSE — the MOST ABUNDANT organic polymer on Earth (~50 billion tonnes produced annually by plants). Chemically: a long, UNBRANCHED chain of thousands of β-D-GLUCOSE units linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. Glucose chains hydrogen-bond to form MICROFIBRILS → fibres → layered into the plant CELL WALL. Cellulose provides: (a) STRUCTURAL rigidity (plants stand upright because of cellulose + lignin); (b) PROTECTION from pathogens; (c) SHAPE. HUMANS cannot digest cellulose (no cellulase enzyme) — it acts as DIETARY FIBRE, adding bulk to stool, promoting gut health. COWS, BUFFALOES, RUMINANTS digest cellulose via SYMBIOTIC microbes (bacteria + protozoa in the rumen) that produce cellulase. Termites, wood-eating insects, some fungi also digest cellulose via microbial symbionts. ECONOMIC USES: (1) WOOD — cellulose + lignin + hemicellulose; basis of construction, furniture, fuel. (2) PAPER — cellulose fibres from wood pulp. (3) COTTON — 90% cellulose; textile. (4) LINEN — from flax (Linum). (5) JUTE — from Corchorus; 'golden fibre'; world's 2nd most produced natural fibre. (6) RAYON, VISCOSE — regenerated cellulose fibres; semi-synthetic. (7) CELLOPHANE — transparent film. (8) NITROCELLULOSE — explosives, early films. (9) CELLULOSE ACETATE — photographic film, cigarette filters. OTHER major PLANT POLYSACCHARIDES: (1) STARCH — α-1,4 glucose chains (amylose, linear) + branched chains (amylopectin, α-1,6 branches); ENERGY STORAGE in plants; found in potato tubers, rice, wheat, maize grains, pulses; DIGESTIBLE by humans (salivary + pancreatic amylase). (2) HEMICELLULOSE — mixed sugars; plant cell wall. (3) PECTIN — galacturonic acid polymer; gives jellies/jams their gel; abundant in citrus peel, apple, guava. (4) INULIN — fructose polymer; in chicory, jerusalem artichoke. (5) LIGNIN — not a polysaccharide but a complex AROMATIC polymer; gives wood its hardness + brown colour. ANIMALS store GLYCOGEN (like amylopectin, more branched) in liver + muscle. Fungi + arthropod exoskeletons use CHITIN (N-acetylglucosamine polymer).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a dicotyledonous plant (dicot)?

options.option_text: WHEAT — it's a MONOCOT (grass family Poaceae); has 1 cotyledon, parallel-veined leaves, fibrous roots

questions.explanation: DICOTS vs MONOCOTS — two great classes of ANGIOSPERMS. DICOTS (Dicotyledonae / Magnoliopsida — ~2,00,000 species): (a) Seeds with 2 COTYLEDONS; (b) Leaves with RETICULATE (net-like) VENATION; (c) TAP ROOT system; (d) Flower parts in 4s or 5s; (e) Vascular bundles in stem arranged in RING, with open (cambium present → secondary growth / wood possible); (f) Pollen with 3 furrows. EXAMPLES: mango, neem, rose, apple, pea, bean, mustard, sunflower, cotton, tomato, brinjal, potato, pulses, most trees (peepal, banyan), hibiscus. MONOCOTS (Monocotyledonae / Liliopsida — ~70,000 species): (a) Seed with 1 COTYLEDON; (b) Leaves with PARALLEL VENATION; (c) FIBROUS ROOT system (adventitious); (d) Flower parts in 3s (or multiples); (e) Vascular bundles SCATTERED in stem, closed (no cambium → no secondary growth normally, hence palms/grasses don't form 'wood'); (f) Pollen with 1 pore. EXAMPLES: wheat, rice, maize (corn), barley, oat (ALL grasses, family POACEAE), sugarcane, bamboo, onion, garlic, lily, tulip, orchid, BANANA, palm, coconut, DATE palm, ginger, turmeric, pineapple. KEY EXAM DIFFERENTIATOR: RICE, WHEAT, MAIZE, SUGARCANE, BANANA, ONION, PALM are MONOCOTS — common food grains/staples. Pea, mustard, bean, mango, apple are DICOTS. BIGGEST plant family on Earth: ASTERACEAE (Compositae) — sunflower family, ~25,000 species; then ORCHIDACEAE (orchids, ~28,000 species actually largest). POACEAE (Grass family) — most ECONOMICALLY IMPORTANT (rice, wheat, maize, barley, oat, rye, millet, sorghum — feed most humans; plus bamboo, sugarcane). BRASSICACEAE (mustard family): cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli, radish, turnip, mustard — all Brassica. FABACEAE / LEGUMINOSAE (legumes/pulses): pea, bean, lentil, soy, groundnut, chickpea, gram — with N-fixing root nodules (Rhizobium). SOLANACEAE (nightshade family): tomato, potato, brinjal, chilli, tobacco. ROSACEAE: rose, apple, pear, peach, strawberry. RUTACEAE: citrus (orange, lemon, lime). CUCURBITACEAE: cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, bottle gourd. LILIACEAE: onion, garlic, lily, tulip. MUSACEAE: banana, plantain.
